conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I spend my days talking with brand-new moms about the emotional ups and downs that can come after a baby arrives. I know you’ve got a lot on your plate right now, so I appreciate you taking a few quiet minutes for yourself.

Today we’re going to use a short questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply a 10-question check-in that helps us spot how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past week. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything we discuss stays between you, me, and the clinical team—you have my word on confidentiality. We’ll just have a relaxed conversation; I’ll re-word each item so it feels more natural, and you can answer in whatever way feels most comfortable.

Whenever you’re ready, we’ll start with the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to look forward to things, or have you found yourself not really enjoying the little moments that used to make you smile?

I guess… I don’t get excited the way I used to. Even little things—like my favorite coffee or a funny show—just feel flat. I’ll try to watch something or scroll my phone while the baby naps, but it’s like I’m just going through the motions. Nothing brings that spark anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can still laugh sometimes—like when my sister sent that silly meme—but it feels kind of forced. Most of the time the funny side just slips past me. I’ll smile because I know I’m supposed to, but the laughter doesn’t come easily or feel real deep down.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I keep thinking I should be excited about stuff—like when my mom offers to come over so I can take a walk or grab a coffee—but even that feels like one more chore. I used to love planning little outings, and now it’s like, “What’s the point?” I do them anyway, but the happy buzz never shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty much every day. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe my milk isn’t enough or I missed his sleepy cue. Last night he wouldn’t settle for two hours and I kept replaying everything I’d done, convinced it was my fault for not reading him properly. My head knows babies just cry, but I still feel like I’m failing him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

All the time. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s not breathing right—even though he’s perfectly fine. Or I’ll lie down and picture dropping him, or the stroller rolling into the street. I know it’s irrational, but I can’t shake the fear something awful is about to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes—those waves come out of nowhere. The other night I was just rocking the baby in the nursery and suddenly felt like I couldn’t breathe, like the walls were closing in. My chest got tight, my hands shook, and I had to put him in the bassinet for a second so I could sit on the floor and gulp air. It passed after a few minutes, but I was still trembling and watching the monitor like something terrible might happen.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like as soon as I finish one feed, the next is due, or there’s laundry piled up, bottles to wash, texts to answer…and I can’t keep up. I end up crying while I fold onesies because it seems like the mess multiplies the second I look away. I keep telling myself millions of moms handle this, but right now it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening a lot. Even when the baby’s finally down and the house is quiet, my mind just keeps spinning—replaying every little thing I think I did wrong, worrying something will happen to him, feeling guilty that I’m not happier. I’ll lie there for an hour or two before I finally drift off, and then I jerk awake at every tiny sound, heart pounding, sure something’s wrong.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. There’s this heavy, sad feeling that’s just… there. I’ll be holding the baby and tears start rolling down my face out of nowhere. I look at his little face and feel guilty because I’m supposed to be happy, but instead I feel empty and weepy. It’s like a gray cloud parked itself over me and won’t budge.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s like once I start, I can’t stop. Yesterday I cried because I spilled pumped milk on the counter—just stood there sobbing over those two ounces like it was the end of the world. And then I felt ridiculous for crying, which made me cry harder. It happens almost every day now; the tears just build up and overflow.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get overwhelmed and feel like I’m failing, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby deserves.

It sounds like you've been carrying a very heavy emotional load since your baby arrived. You shared that nearly every day feels clouded by sadness, worry, and a sense that even simple joys have vanished. You described feeling overwhelmed by everyday tasks, nightly racing thoughts, sudden panic, and frequent tears, all while trying to be the mother you want to be. These feelings are understandably exhausting and can make the early postpartum weeks feel even harder.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter feels forced and is noticeably diminished, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing activities as chores and stating "the happy buzz never shows up," aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself "pretty much every day" and gives a vivid recent example of self-blame when the baby fussed, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports constant, intrusive, irrational fears occurring 'all the time,' matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intense, sudden panic symptoms (breathlessness, chest tightness, trembling) that arose unexpectedly while doing routine baby care, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to keep up, and tearful collapse—semantic match for “most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all.”</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to racing, guilt-laden thoughts and hyper-arousal, matching "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness, tearfulness, and persistent low mood that aligns with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily crying episodes that feel uncontrollable and disproportionate, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 26 places well above the 13-point threshold indicating probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset. The patient endorses <sym>markedly diminished interest or pleasure</sym> (Q2 score 3), <sym>daily low mood</sym> and <sym>frequent crying</sym> (Q8, Q9 scores 3), <sym>unwarranted self-blame</sym> (Q3 score 3), <sym>significant anxiety</sym> and <sym>sudden panic</sym> (Q4, Q5 scores 3), and <sym>sleep disruption beyond infant care</sym> (Q7 score 3). These responses align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder</med> and suggest co-occurring <med>anxiety disorder</med>. No self-harm ideation is present (Q10 score 0). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Ask your clinician to rule out <med>bipolar disorder</med> with a validated tool (e.g. MDQ) before starting antidepressant therapy
3. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> focusing on postpartum challenges
4. Plan daily 15-30 minute support blocks (partner, family, or friend) to allow restorative sleep or rest
5. Practice brief grounding techniques (slow breathing, 5-4-3-2-1 sensory check) when panic sensations start
6. Limit information overload-choose one trusted parenting resource and set social-media boundaries to reduce comparison stress
7. Keep the next pediatric visit; mention mood struggles so your pediatrician can coordinate care with your provider
8. If distress escalates or you develop any thoughts of self-harm, go to the nearest emergency department or call your local mental-health crisis line
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [insert date]  
Source: Self-report on 10-item Edinburgh-based questionnaire

Presenting Concerns  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, and anhedonia (Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Daily guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Marked anxiety with intrusive “what-if” thoughts, nocturnal rumination, and two recent panic episodes (Q4, Q5, Q7)  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed and unable to cope with routine infant tasks (Q6)  
- Sleep initiation and maintenance difficulties unrelated to infant demands (Q7)

Pattern Summary  
Symptoms cluster around depressive (sad mood, loss of pleasure, crying) and anxiety (excessive worry, panic attacks, intrusive catastrophic images) domains. Functional impact evident in self-described “drowning” feeling and impaired enjoyment of motherhood. No current self-harm ideation (Q10); protective factor.

Screening Significance  
High score likelihood on standardized perinatal mood measures; clinical interview warranted to evaluate for Major Depressive Episode with Peripartum Onset and comorbid Anxiety Disorder. Safety plan discussion recommended given intensity of distress and panic symptoms.
